record.original_question: Let (W1,S1) and (W2,S2) be Coxeter systems, and let u,v in W1 and w,z in W2 be such that the Bruhat intervals [u,v] and [w,z] are isomorphic as posets. Must the corresponding Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials agree, i.e. must P_{u,v}(q) = P_{w,z}(q)?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 1.4. Let (W1,S1), (W2,S2) be two Coxeter systems, and u,v in W1, w,z in W2 be such that [u,v] ~= [w,z] (isomorphic as posets). Then P_{u,v}(q) = P_{w,z}(q).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $(W_1, S_1)$ and $(W_2, S_2)$ be two Coxeter systems. Recall that for a Coxeter system $(W, S)$, the Bruhat order $\le$ on $W$ is the partial order generated by declaring $u \le v$ whenever some reduced expression for $v$ contains a reduced expression for $u$ as a subword; for $u \le v$ in $W$, the Bruhat interval $[u,v]$ is the poset $\{x \in W : u \le x \le v\}$. To each pair $u \le v$ in a Coxeter system one associates the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial $P_{u,v}(q) \in \mathbb{Z}[q]$, the unique polynomial of degree at most $(\ell(v) - \ell(u) - 1)/2$ (with $P_{u,u}=1$) defined by the recursion arising from the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of the Hecke algebra of $(W,S)$.

Suppose $u, v \in W_1$ and $w, z \in W_2$ satisfy $u \le v$, $w \le z$, and there is an isomorphism of posets $[u,v] \cong [w,z]$. Prove or disprove: under these hypotheses one always has
$$P_{u,v}(q) = P_{w,z}(q).$$

status_evidence.title: Combinatorial Invariance Conjecture
status_evidence.snippet: The combinatorial invariance conjecture of Lusztig and Dyer states that the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial depends only on the isomorphism type of the Bruhat interval; it remains open in general.
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture is widely known to be open.

status_evidence.title: Advancing mathematics by guiding human intuition with AI (Davies et al., Nature 2021; Blundell et al.)
status_evidence.snippet: Progress on the combinatorial invariance conjecture for symmetric groups via a conjectural formula based on hypercube decompositions.
status_evidence.claim: Recent progress has been made for symmetric groups but the full conjecture remains unproven.

artifact.status_search_result: The statement is the Combinatorial Invariance Conjecture of Lusztig and Dyer, formulated in the 1980s. It remains open in general. Significant progress has been made in special cases (e.g., for lower intervals in the symmetric group via hypercube decompositions, including work motivated by DeepMind collaborations), but no proof for arbitrary Coxeter systems has been established.
